1) Some oblivious transfer protocols and some of their derivatives, and also some non-interactive ZK arguments are subject to a semi-honest attack, which allows the verifier to derive bounds for some of the sender (prover) inputs.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following issues: (a) the additional property that the decryption of some semantically secure homomophic encryption schemes possess, (b) the effect of the size of the plaintext space on the security of the protocols, and (c) the fix that prevents the attacks.
the following question: what happens when the inputs of an oblivious transfer protocol or a zero-knowledge argument are not uniformly distributed in the plaintext space?
the following questions: 1) Is there an attack on some oblivious transfer protocols that are based on semantically secure homomorphism schemes?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

if a homomorphic encryption scheme has the property that the decryption also reveals a random coin, and if the plaintext space is much larger than the space of possible inputs, then the scheme is not secure in the sense of oblivious transfer or zero-knowledge.
if the random coin can be derived from the ciphertext then the protocol should be modified so that the ciphertext does not reveal the random coin.

the protocols we consider are secure if the underlying semantically secure encryption scheme is secure against chosen-plaintext attacks, and if the sender's (resp. prover's) input space is large enough.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the oblivious transfer protocol of Naor and Pinkas [1] is secure only against malicious choosers, but not against semi-honest ones.

we show a weakness in some oblivious transfer protocols that use semantically secure homomorphism encryption underneath, and that the same weakness can be applied to their derivatives and to some non-Interactive zero-knowledge proofs.
we show that some protocols are not secure even if the underlying encryption scheme is semantically secure.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the random coins used for the encryption of the sender's or prover inputs in oblivious transfer protocols and zero-knowledge arguments should be kept secret.
in some cases the random coin used in encryption may be considered a part of the plaintext and thus it should be protected as well.

when a semantically secure encryption scheme is used as a building block in a cryptographic protocol, the security analysis should not only focus on the security of the underlying encryption scheme, but also on the properties of the plaintext space and the decryption function.
